Miami's Cuban restaurant scene stands as a living monument to the waves of immigration that have reshaped the city since the 1960s. According to Eater Miami, Cuban food in Miami isn't merely a cuisine option among many—it represents the daily heartbeat of the city and a fundamental part of its cultural identity. The immigrant families who arrived during this transformative period didn't simply bring recipes; they established a comprehensive food culture that has become inseparable from what it means to live in Miami today.

The neighborhood of Little Havana exemplifies this culinary legacy. Home to many Cuban exiles and immigrants from Central and South America, Little Havana was named after Havana, Cuba's capital and largest city, serving as both a physical and symbolic anchor for the community's food traditions. Within and beyond this neighborhood, Cuban restaurants have proliferated, each carrying forward family recipes, cooking techniques, and the stories of resilience that define the immigrant experience.

Cuban cuisine itself reflects the island's geographic position and multicultural history, blending Spanish, African, and Caribbean influences into a distinctive flavor profile. Staples like ropa vieja, mofongo, and Cuban sandwiches have become so embedded in Miami's food culture that they function as markers of local identity. For many Miami residents, eating Cuban food isn't a special occasion—it's the ordinary rhythm of daily life, a constant connection to heritage and home.

They also function as cultural anchors, spaces where language, tradition, and memory are actively sustained and transmitted to younger generations who may not have direct experience of Cuba itself.

Eater Miami's guide arrives at a moment when food journalism increasingly recognizes immigrant cuisines not as exotic additions to a city's dining landscape but as foundational elements of place and identity.
